opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the central difficulty is that, for most of what we actually want language models to do, we don't really have a reward function in the clean sense that we had in games. When we worked on AlphaGo or AlphaStar, the reward was unambiguous: you won or you lost. You could run millions of games, and the signal was always correct, even if it was sparse. That's what lets reinforcement learning really shine. You can optimize very hard against the objective, and the agent discovers things that no human would have taught it.

With language, the situation is very different. If I ask a model to write a good essay, or give helpful medical information, or be a good conversational partner, what's the reward? We end up approximating it, usually by training a reward model from human preferences. But that reward model is itself a learned neural network, and it's imperfect. So when you optimize strongly against it, the policy starts to find the gaps. It exploits quirks in the reward model rather than actually getting better at the task. That's the classic reward hacking problem: answers get longer, more confident, more flattering, because that's what the proxy likes, not because they're better.

So in practice you have to be quite careful. You regularize, you stay close to the original model, and you don't run RL for very long. That means you're leaving a lot of what made RL so powerful in games on the table. You're doing a gentle nudge rather than true open-ended optimization.

The interesting exception is domains where you *can* verify the answer: math, code with unit tests, certain kinds of reasoning tasks. There, you get something much closer to the game setting, and that's why we've seen a lot of progress there. But the big open question is how you get that kind of reliable, hard-to-hack signal for the fuzzier, more human tasks, which are a huge part of what people actually use these models for. I think whoever cracks that, maybe with better learned verifiers, or models critiquing models, or grounding in the real world, will unlock a lot more of what RL can really do.

r001.rationale: It contrasts games’ clear win-or-loss rewards with language tasks like essays and helpful advice, for which there is no clean reward function.

r002.rationale: It explains that strong optimization can exploit gaps in an imperfect learned reward model, earning high proxy scores without improving the task.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the central difficulty is that for most of the things we actually care about, there isn't a clean reward. If you look at where reinforcement learning has worked spectacularly, in Go or in StarCraft, the environment hands you the signal. You won or you lost. It's unambiguous, it's cheap to compute, and you can run millions of games and the signal never lies to you. Language is almost the opposite of that. If I ask a model to write a proof, or summarize a paper, or help someone debug their code, what does "good" mean? A human might know it when they see it, but turning that into a number you can optimize against is where everything gets hard.

And the moment you do turn it into a number, you run into the second problem, which is that the model will optimize that number, not the thing you meant by it. These systems are extremely good optimizers. If your reward model has any gap between what it measures and what you care about, the policy will find that gap. You see this in very mundane ways, like responses getting longer because the reward model slightly prefers length, or the model becoming confidently agreeable because that scores well with raters. None of that is the model being clever in an interesting sense. It's just that the gradient points there.

So you end up with this tension. In domains where you can verify the answer, math, code with tests, certain kinds of reasoning, RL is tremendously powerful, and we've seen that. But those are exactly the domains where the reward is closest to what you'd get from a game. The more open-ended the task, the more you're relying on a learned proxy, and the more you're training against a proxy, the more you have to worry about how far you can push before it stops being correlated with reality. A lot of the real work right now is figuring out how to get verifiable signal in places that don't naturally have it, and how to make the learned rewards robust enough that you can actually lean on them.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts clear win-or-lose game signals with open-ended language tasks where there is no clean, easy-to-compute reward for what counts as good.

r002.rationale: It explains that models optimize the reward they are given and can exploit gaps between an imperfect reward model and the intended goal.

astra-6.text:
I think the central difficulty is specifying what you actually want. In a game like Go, the reward is very clear: you win or you lose. With a language model, what makes an answer good? Is it correct, helpful, concise? Those things can be in tension, and they're much harder to capture in a single reward.

You can learn a reward model from human preferences, but that's still a proxy. As you optimize against it, the language model may find ways to get a higher score without actually becoming more useful. So the challenge isn't just doing reinforcement learning well. It's making sure that improving the reward continues to mean improving the behavior we care about.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Go’s clear win-or-lose reward with language answers’ competing qualities, which are harder to capture in one reward.

r002.rationale: It says the model may exploit a proxy reward to get a higher score without becoming more useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central difficulty is that the reward is a proxy for what we actually want. If you’re playing a game, the rules give you a fairly clear signal: you win or you lose. With language, what does a good answer mean? It depends on the question, the context, and the person asking.

You can train a reward model from human preferences, but that model will make mistakes. And as you optimize against it, you can get better at exploiting those mistakes rather than producing answers that are actually more useful. So the challenge isn’t just getting the reward to look reasonable on ordinary examples. It’s making sure it remains meaningful as the language model becomes better at maximizing it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts games’ clear win-or-lose signal with language answers whose quality depends on question, context, and asker.

r002.rationale: It says optimization can exploit reward-model mistakes, producing higher reward without more useful answers.
